To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the spin evolution of a pulsar with a superfluid core is qualitatively similar to that of a pulsar in the crustal magnetosphere model.

(1) the spin evolution of the star is determined by the interplay between the magnetic field and the superfluid component, and the latter is the dominant factor in determining the braking index, n; (2) the superfluid component is responsible for a spin-up phase of the star after which the braking index decreases toward a value n ~ 2; and (3) the spin-up phase can be observed in the millisecond pulsar sector of the P-P diagram.

(a) the braking index of pulsars is expected to decay toward values n ~ 3, (b) the magnetic field of a pulsar is expected to decay exponentially toward a residual value, (c) the braking index is not an intrinsic property of a pulsar, and (d) the spin-up phase of pulsars is a natural consequence of the weak magnetic coupling of superfluid interiors.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the braking index n of pulsars is a measure of the degree of coupling between the superfluid and the observable crust, but it cannot be considered a reliable measure of the degree to which the magnetic field of a pulsar is decayed.
the spin-down of a neutron star is a very complex phenomenon, which cannot be understood in the framework of a single physical mechanism.
the braking index of a pulsar is not a reliable indicator of the existence of a superfluid component in its interior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a pulsar is a star with a weakly coupled superfluid interior, and the spin evolution is a complex phenomenon which depends on the magnetic field decay rate and the coupling strength.
the spin evolution of the pulsar is not necessarily determined only by the magnetic field of a neutron star, but it could be affected also by the presence of superfluids in the star's interior.
the superfluid interior of a pulsar is coupled to the crust only on very long, spin-down, time scales, and that the observed braking indices are a result of this coupling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spin-down of pulsars with weakly coupled superfluids could be significantly slower than the spin-down of ordinary pulsars.
the braking indices of pulsars are not expected to be constant in time and that the values observed in the present sample are not necessarily indicative of the asymptotic values of n.
a weak coupling between the superfluid and the crust could explain a large number of the observed braking indices of young pulsars, including the values n < 2.5.
